title: What happens if a consumer crashes after consuming but before committing the offset, and how do you ensure at-least-once (manual offset commit)?
shortTitle: What happens if a consumer crashes after consuming but before committing the offset, and how do you ensure at-least-once?

s1_definition.profdef: If a consumer reads records and crashes before committing their offsets, the committed offset still points before those records, so when the consumer or another group member resumes, it re-reads and reprocesses them. This is at-least-once delivery: no message is lost, but a message can be processed more than once. You ensure at-least-once deliberately by disabling auto-commit and committing offsets manually only after processing has succeeded, and you make the downstream processing idempotent so reprocessing a duplicate has no harmful effect.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine a settlement clerk at National Bank of India who takes a stack of transfer slips off the tray, starts working, but faints before marking the tray as cleared up to that slip. When a new clerk arrives, the tray still shows those slips as not yet cleared, so the new clerk picks them up again. Nothing is lost, but a slip might get worked twice, so the ledger must be designed so that applying the same transfer twice does not double-charge Rajesh. The safe rule is: only mark the tray cleared after the work is truly done.
s1_definition.oneliner: A crash before commit means those records are reprocessed on resume, which is at-least-once, so you disable auto-commit, commit only after successful processing, and make processing idempotent.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** If a consumer reads records and crashes before committing their offsets, the committed offset still points before those records, so when the consumer or another group member resumes, it re-reads and reprocesses them. This is at-least-once delivery: no message is lost, but a message can be processed more than once. You ensure at-least-once deliberately by disabling auto-commit and committing offsets manually only after processing has succeeded, and you make the downstream processing idempotent so reprocessing a duplicate has no harmful effect.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine a settlement clerk at National Bank of India who takes a stack of transfer slips off the tray, starts working, but faints before marking the tray as cleared up to that slip. When a new clerk arrives, the tray still shows those slips as not yet cleared, so the new clerk picks them up again. Nothing is lost, but a slip might get worked twice, so the ledger must be designed so that applying the same transfer twice does not double-charge Rajesh. The safe rule is: only mark the tray cleared after the work is truly done.

**One line to remember:** A crash before commit means those records are reprocessed on resume, which is at-least-once, so you disable auto-commit, commit only after successful processing, and make processing idempotent.

sections.s2_technical:
Kafka tracks each consumer group's position per partition as a committed offset stored in the internal offsets topic. A record is only considered done when its offset is committed. So if a consumer polls records at offsets 50 through 59, begins processing, and crashes at offset 55 before committing, the committed offset is still 50. When the group rebalances and another member or the restarted consumer takes over that partition, it resumes from offset 50 and reprocesses 50 through 59. The records are not lost, but some are processed twice.

The default behaviour makes this worse if misunderstood. With `enable.auto.commit=true`, the consumer commits offsets automatically on a timer controlled by `auto.commit.interval.ms`, by default every five seconds. The danger is that auto-commit can commit offsets for records you have polled but not yet finished processing, which can cause message loss if you crash after the auto-commit but before processing, because on resume those records are skipped. So auto-commit gives you a weak guarantee that is neither clean at-least-once nor exactly-once.

To get reliable at-least-once, you turn off auto-commit with `props.put("enable.auto.commit", "false")` and commit manually after processing succeeds. You poll a batch, process each record fully, including any database write, and only then call `consumer.commitSync()`, which blocks until the commit is acknowledged, or `consumer.commitAsync()` for lower latency with a callback to handle failures. Because you commit after processing, a crash before the commit simply means the batch is reprocessed on resume, so nothing is lost. The cost is possible duplicates, which is the defining tradeoff of at-least-once.

Since duplicates are possible, idempotent processing is essential. You design the downstream so that applying the same record twice has the same effect as applying it once. In banking you do this with an idempotency key, often the transfer id, and a processed-ids table or a unique constraint, so a second attempt to settle the same transfer is detected and skipped. Alternatively the operation itself is naturally idempotent, such as setting a balance to an absolute value computed from an authoritative source rather than incrementing.

A senior nuance is where you commit relative to external writes. If you commit before writing to the database, a crash in between loses the effect of the record even though the offset moved, which is at-most-once and unsafe. If you write to the database and then commit, a crash in between reprocesses, which is at-least-once and safe when idempotent. For true exactly-once you need Kafka transactions that commit the output and the offset atomically, or an idempotent sink. Another nuance is commit granularity: committing per record is slow, so you usually commit per batch after processing the whole batch, accepting that a crash reprocesses the whole batch. A final nuance is handling `commitAsync` failures and doing a final `commitSync` on shutdown or rebalance via a rebalance listener.
sections.s3_banking:
National Bank of India runs a settlement consumer that reads transfer events and applies them to the ledger. A crash must never lose a transfer, and reprocessing must never double-charge a customer.

Problem 1 — with auto-commit, the consumer might commit offsets before the transfer is applied, so a crash could skip a transfer and lose Rajesh's money movement. This is exactly why auto-commit is disabled for reliable delivery.

Problem 2 — if the consumer crashes after applying a transfer but before committing, the transfer is reprocessed on resume. This is exactly at-least-once: safe from loss but prone to duplicates.

Problem 3 — a reprocessed transfer must not settle twice. This is exactly what idempotent processing with an idempotency key and a processed-ids set solves.

The code will show a manual-commit consumer that applies a transfer to a ledger, records the transfer id to prevent duplicates, and commits only after success, with a simulated crash before commit to show the reprocess-without-double-charge behaviour for Rajesh and Priya.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a batch of transfer events including TXF-00042, Rajesh (SAV2001) to Priya (CUR3001) for fifty thousand rupees, at offset 55 in the partition.

Step 1 — the consumer polls the batch with auto-commit disabled. The committed offset is still 50 from the previous batch.

Step 2 — the consumer processes each record by applying the transfer to the idempotent ledger and recording its transfer id. When it reaches TXF-00042, the ledger applies it and records the id.

Step 3 — right after applying TXF-00042, the consumer crashes before calling commit. Because the offset was never committed, Kafka still has the committed offset at 50.

Step 4 — on restart, the group resumes from offset 50 and reprocesses the whole batch, including TXF-00042. Nothing is lost, which is the at-least-once guarantee.

Step 5 — when reprocessing reaches TXF-00042, the ledger sees the transfer id is already recorded and skips it, so Rajesh is not charged twice. Only after the whole batch processes cleanly does the consumer commit, moving the offset forward.

```
2026-10-24 23:10:01 [INFO] Applied TXF-00041
2026-10-24 23:10:01 [INFO] Applied TXF-00042
2026-10-24 23:10:01 [SEVERE] CRASH before commit! Offset NOT committed → batch will reprocess
--- restart ---
2026-10-24 23:10:05 [INFO] Skipped duplicate TXF-00041
2026-10-24 23:10:05 [INFO] Skipped duplicate TXF-00042
2026-10-24 23:10:05 [INFO] Offsets committed after successful processing
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  committed offset = 50
    │
    ▼
  poll() → records 50..59 (auto-commit OFF)
    │
    ▼
  process each: applyTransfer(transferId) → ledger + record id
    │
    │   reach offset 55 (TXF-00042): applied, id recorded
    ▼
  CRASH before commitSync()   (offset still 50)
    │
    ▼
  restart / rebalance → resume from offset 50 (NO loss)
    │
    ▼
  reprocess 50..59
    ├─ already-processed ids → SKIP (no double charge)  ← idempotency
    └─ new ids → apply
    │
    ▼
  commitSync() AFTER full batch → committed offset = 60

  Guarantee: at-least-once (no loss, possible duplicate → made safe by idempotency)
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Kafka records a consumer group's position as a committed offset, and a record is only considered done once its offset is committed. So if a consumer polls a batch, starts processing, and crashes before committing, the committed offset still points before that batch, and when the consumer or another group member resumes, it re-reads and reprocesses those records. Nothing is lost, but some records are processed more than once, and that is exactly the definition of at-least-once delivery.

The common mistake is relying on auto-commit, which commits on a timer and can commit offsets for records you have polled but not finished processing, which risks losing a record if you crash after the auto-commit. So for reliable at-least-once I disable auto-commit and commit manually only after processing succeeds. I poll a batch, process each record fully including the database write, and only then call commit-sync. Because the commit happens after processing, a crash before it simply causes a clean reprocess on resume.

Since duplicates are now possible, I make the processing idempotent. In banking I use an idempotency key, usually the transfer id, with a processed-ids table or a unique constraint, so a second attempt to settle the same transfer is detected and skipped. The ordering that matters is process, then persist, then commit the offset; committing before persisting would be at-most-once and could lose money, which is never acceptable.

In my National Bank of India settlement service, we disabled auto-commit and committed offsets only after applying each transfer to the ledger, and we keyed the ledger on the transfer id so reprocessing after a crash never double-charged customers like Rajesh. When we needed true exactly-once rather than at-least-once with idempotency, we moved to Kafka transactions that commit the output records and the consumer offsets atomically, but for most of our pipelines at-least-once with idempotent processing was the right, simpler choice.
